# What is IGV? {.section-slide background-color="#13294b"}

[Episode 01]{.ep-num}

[What is a genome browser, and when would I use one?]{.ep-q}

## A genome browser

Instead of scrolling through millions of lines of text, **scroll and zoom along a chromosome** and see data line up against the reference.

IGV (Broad Institute) is popular because it:

- runs **locally** — your data never leaves your machine
- reads **only the region you are viewing**, so big files load fast
- supports dozens of **file formats**
- stacks data as **tracks** for side-by-side comparison

## Why look at your data?

::: {.incremental}
- **Spot problems early** — misaligned reads, coverage gaps, wrong reference
- **Real signal or artifact?** — a heterozygous SNP vs. strand bias or low base quality
- **Build confidence** before spending time on downstream analysis
:::

. . .

::: {.muted .small}
IGV *visualizes* the output of your pipelines (alignment, variant calling, …) — it does not do the processing.
:::

## What can IGV show?

![](../fig/intro-01-igv-use-cases.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Epigenomic signal · NGS alignments · RNA-seq · Variants & genotypes — we'll see all four today
:::

## File formats we'll use

| Format | Contains |
|:-------|:---------|
| **FASTA** (+ `.fai`) | Reference genome sequence |
| **BED** | Genomic intervals — genes, SNP calls |
| **BAM** (+ `.bai`) | Aligned sequencing reads |
| **TDF** | Precomputed coverage |
| **VCF** | Variant calls & sample genotypes |

::: {.muted .small}
Plus many more — BAM, CRAM, bigWig, GFF/GTF, …
:::

## Your turn: launch IGV {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Open IGV on your computer. You should see a genome drop-down (e.g. `Human hg19`) in the top left, a chromosome ideogram, and an empty track area.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
If IGV doesn't start, check you downloaded the right build for your OS — and put up your hand!
:::

# IGV Basics {.section-slide background-color="#0f8b8d"}

[Episode 02]{.ep-num}

[How do I load data and move around the genome?]{.ep-q}

## Load a genome and data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../fig/basics-01-load-server-data.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. Genome drop-down → **Human hg19**
2. [File > Load from Server…]{.menu}
3. Expand **Tutorials** → tick **UI Basics (Encode)**

<br>

Loads four ENCODE ChIP-seq tracks (histone modifications).

::: {.small .muted}
⚠️ Expand *Tutorials* — don't tick the box next to it, or you'll load everything!
:::
:::
::::

## More hosted genomes

![](../fig/basics-08-more-hosted-genomes.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Genome drop-down → **More…** for bacteria, model organisms, other builds
:::

## Four zoom levels

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/basics-02-whole-genome-chromosome.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
| Level | How |
|:--|:--|
| **Whole genome** | Chromosome menu → **All**, or *Home* |
| **Chromosome** | Pick **chr1**, or click **1** on the ruler |
| **Region** | Drag on the ruler; double-click a track |
| **Base pair** | Keep zooming, or use the zoom widget |

::: {.small}
Alt-click zooms back out
:::
:::
::::

## Getting around

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/basics-03-zoom-navigate.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
**Move without zooming**

- Click the **cytoband** to jump
- **Click and drag** in the data panel to scroll

**Jump straight there**

- Type a locus: `chr1:144,874,969-145,000,000`
- …or a gene name: `NRAS` → **Go**
:::
::::

## Your turn: find NRAS {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Starting from the **whole-genome** view, go to **chr1**, then search for `NRAS`.

Keep zooming until you can read **individual bases**.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Search takes you to the whole gene. Drag on the ruler, double-click, or use **+** until letters appear in the sequence track.
:::

## Sequence & gene tracks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/basics-04-sequence-gene-track.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
**Sequence track**

- One base per column once zoomed in
- Arrow → switch strand
- Click → 3-frame translation

**Gene track**

- Line = intron · thick block = exon · thinner end blocks = UTRs
- Right-click → **Collapsed / Expanded / Squished**
:::
::::

## Your turn: gene display modes {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Go to `EGFR`. Right-click the *RefSeq genes* track and try **Collapsed**, **Expanded** and **Squished**.

What is the trade-off?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
**Collapsed** — compact, can't tell transcripts apart. **Expanded** — one transcript per row, easiest to read, uses the most space. **Squished** — one per row but thin: fits many, harder to read.
:::

## Combining data tracks

[Tools > Combine Data Tracks]{.menu} — add, subtract, multiply or divide two numeric tracks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/basics-06-combine-tracks-dialog.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/basics-07-combine-tracks-result.png)
:::
::::

## Your turn: combine two tracks {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Add two of the ENCODE ChIP-seq tracks together. How does the combined track compare to its two sources?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
The **Sum** track peaks wherever *either* source peaks, with height equal to the total signal — one track to read instead of two.
:::

# Loading Your Own Genome {.section-slide background-color="#13294b"}

[Episode 03]{.ep-num}

[How do I view a genome that isn't built into IGV?]{.ep-q}

## Genome from a FASTA file

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/load-genome-from-file.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
1. [File > New Session]{.menu} to clear
2. [Genomes > Load Genome from File…]{.menu}
3. Open `igvData/genome/chr1.fasta`

<br>

Now there's **no gene track** and **no cytoband** — just sequence.

4. [File > Load from File…]{.menu} → `refSeq_chr1.bed`
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Note the menus: Genomes menu for the genome, File menu for tracks.
:::

## Your turn: search by gene name {.exercise}

::: {.task}
**Before** loading `refSeq_chr1.bed`, search for `CAP9`. What happens?

Now load the BED file and try again.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Without annotation IGV doesn't know where genes are — only coordinates work. With the BED file loaded, the search jumps straight to the gene.
:::

. . .

::: {.small .muted}
Annotation BED files like this can be downloaded from the UCSC Table Browser. Cytobands can't be added separately.
:::

# Alignments & SNPs {.section-slide background-color="#0f8b8d"}

[Episode 04]{.ep-num}

[How can I tell a real SNP from an artifact?]{.ep-q}

## Paired-end reads

![](../fig/snps-00-ngs-paired-end.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Each fragment is read from both ends · distance between outer edges = **insert size**
:::

## The SAM / BAM format

![](../fig/snps-00-sambam-format.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Read name · position · **mapping quality** · **CIGAR** · mate info · sequence & base qualities
:::

## Load reads and SNP calls

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/snps-01-load-navigate.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
[File > Load from File…]{.menu} in `igvData/snps/`:

- `snp_calls.bed` — two candidate SNPs
- `NA12878.SLX.sample.bam`

Search `snp1` → **Go**

::: {.small .muted}
Load only the `.bam` — IGV finds the `.bai` index automatically if it's next to it.
:::
:::
::::

## Sort by base

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/snps-02-sort-quality.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Centre the mismatch between the guide lines
- Right-click → **Sort alignments by › base**
- Hover the **coverage bar** for allele counts

<br>

**A real het SNP looks like:** a consistent mismatch in ~50% of reads, and little noise around it.
:::
::::

## Your turn: compare snp1 & snp2 {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Go to `snp2`. Compare it with `snp1` — look at how **bright** the mismatched bases are.

Toggle **Shade base by quality** off and on.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
At `snp2` many mismatches are faint → **low base quality**. With shading off they look just as convincing, which is misleading. First warning sign that `snp2` isn't real.
:::

## Sort & colour by strand

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/snps-03-sort-color-strand.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
Right-click →

- **Sort alignments by › read strand**
- **Color alignments by › read strand**

<br>

Non-strand-specific library → expect a **50/50 split**.

A real variant appears on **both** strands. On one strand only = 🚩 artifact.
:::
::::

## Your turn: real or artifact? {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Use strand sorting and colouring on `snp2`. The library was **not** strand-specific.

What do you conclude?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
The mismatches sit on one strand only → likely a **false positive**. Together with the low base quality, that's two independent pieces of evidence against it.
:::

## BLAT: is the read really from here? {.stack}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/snps-04-blat-investigate-peak.png){height="270"}

![](../fig/snps-05-blat-read-sequence-menu.png){height="270"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
A suspiciously narrow coverage spike?

Right-click a read → **BLAT read sequence**

<br>

- One clear best hit → trustworthy
- Many hits with similar scores → **repetitive sequence**, treat with suspicion
:::
::::

## BLAT results

![](../fig/snps-06-blat-results-many-hits.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Many equally good hits across chromosomes → the read can't be placed confidently
:::

# Precomputing Coverage {.section-slide background-color="#13294b"}

[Episode 05]{.ep-num}

[Why does my coverage disappear when I zoom out?]{.ep-q}

## The problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/coverage-01-igvtools-count.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
Zoom all the way out → *"Zoom in to see coverage"*

IGV computes BAM coverage **on the fly** — too slow for a whole chromosome.

**Fix:** precompute it once with igvtools

1. [Tools > Run igvtools…]{.menu}
2. Command: **Count**
3. Input: `NA12878.SLX.sample.bam` → **Run**
:::
::::

## Attach the TDF file

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/coverage-02-load-precomputed.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
Right-click the coverage track →
**Load pre-computed coverage data…**

Pick `NA12878.SLX.sample.bam.tdf`

<br>

Three coverage spikes appear across chr1 — the workshop BAM only contains reads in these regions.
:::
::::

## Your turn: zoom back in {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Zoom in on the **leftmost** spike until you reach base-pair resolution. Where do you land?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Back at `snp1`! Same reads — the coverage is just computed differently depending on zoom level.
:::

# RNA-seq & Splicing {.section-slide background-color="#0f8b8d"}

[Episode 06]{.ep-num}

[How do I compare splicing between tissues?]{.ep-q}

## Why RNA-seq reads look "split"

![](../fig/rnaseq-00-splicing-to-igv.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Reads come from spliced mRNA, but the genome still has introns → a read spanning two exons aligns as a **gapped** alignment
:::

## Set up and load

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/rnaseq-01-preferences-load.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
1. [View > Preferences > Alignments]{.menu}
   tick **Splice Junction Track**
2. Genome **Human hg19**
3. [File > Load from Server…]{.menu}
   Tutorials → **RNA-Seq (Body Map)**

<br>

Two tissues: **heart** and **liver**
:::
::::

## Coverage and junctions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/rnaseq-02-jump-gene-squished.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
Search `SLC25A3`

For each tissue:

- **Coverage** — reads per position
- **Junctions** — arcs joining spliced exons

Right-click RefSeq Genes → **Squished** to see the isoforms
:::
::::

## Your turn: spot the difference {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Zoom in on the **first three exons**. Is there an exon with coverage in one tissue but not the other?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Yes — one tissue has a small coverage bump (an extra exon) that is missing or much lower in the other. That's **tissue-specific alternative splicing**.
:::

## Sashimi plots

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/rnaseq-04-sashimi-plot.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
Right-click junctions → **Sashimi Plot** → tick heart & liver

- **Arcs** = reads across a junction (number = read count)
- **Peaks** = exon coverage

<br>

Right-click → **Set Junction Coverage Min** → `50` to hide low-count junctions
:::
::::

## Your turn: exon 3 {.exercise}

::: {.task}
In the Sashimi plot, zoom to the 5′ end. Compare the heart and liver arcs around **exon 3**.
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
In one tissue an arc **skips** exon 3 (exon 2 → exon 4); in the other, arcs go into and out of exon 3. Read-level evidence that exon 3 is alternatively spliced.
:::

# Variants & Genotypes {.section-slide background-color="#13294b"}

[Episode 07]{.ep-num}

[How can I compare variants across populations?]{.ep-q}

## The dataset

![](../fig/variants-00-the-data.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
1000 Genomes: chromosome 22, ~850 people from populations around the world
:::

## The APOL1 story

![](../fig/variants-00-apol1-background.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Protects against African sleeping sickness · linked to kidney disease (Genovese *et al.*, *Science* 2010)
:::

## Load the session

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/variants-01-load-session-genotypes.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
[File > Open Session…]{.menu}
`igvData/vcf/vcf_session.xml`

Two panels:

- **Variant sites** — one row
- **Genotypes** — one row per sample

A **sample info** colour bar shows metadata such as population.
:::
::::

## Reading the colours {.pair}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/variants-03-allele-color-legend.png){height="300"}

**Variant sites**

[]{.chip style="background:#2b50d8"} reference allele
[]{.chip style="background:#d8322b"} alternate allele
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/variants-04-genotype-color-legend.png){height="300"}

**Genotypes**

[]{.chip style="background:#22d0e0"} homozygous alt
[]{.chip style="background:#2b50d8"} heterozygous
[]{.chip style="background:#c8c8c8"} homozygous ref
:::
::::

## Group by population

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](../fig/variants-02-group-by-population.png){height="540"}
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
1. Search `APOL1:S342G` (gene:protein change!)
2. Right-click genotypes → **Squished**
3. Right-click → **Group By…** → `super_pop`
4. Scroll through the groups

::: {.small .muted}
Sample metadata comes from a separate tab-delimited file whose first column matches the VCF sample names.
:::
:::
::::

## Your turn: population frequencies {.exercise}

::: {.task}
At `APOL1:S342G`, scroll through the population groups.

Is the variant equally common everywhere?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
No — it's absent or rare in most groups and common in **African** populations, matching the selective history of *APOL1*. Grouping makes this visible without computing any frequencies.
:::

# Structural Variants {.section-slide background-color="#0f8b8d"}

[Episode 08]{.ep-num}

[How can paired-end reads reveal deletions, fusions and inversions?]{.ep-q}

## Insert size & orientation

![](../fig/sv-01-paired-end-insert-size.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small .muted style="text-align:center"}
Compare the **inferred** insert size and pair orientation with what we expect — the same evidence SV callers use
:::

## Deletions {.pair}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../fig/sv-02-deletion-red-coloring.png){height="420"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../fig/sv-03-deletion-example.png){height="420"}
:::
::::

Mates land **further apart** than expected → coloured [red]{style="color:#d8322b;font-weight:700"} · coverage drops between the breakpoints

## Inter-chromosomal fusions {.pair}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](../fig/sv-04-fusion-chromosome-colors.png){height="420"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../fig/sv-05-fusion-example.png){height="420"}
:::
::::

Reads coloured by **mate chromosome** cluster at the breakpoint — in the tumour, not the normal

## Inversions {.pair}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/sv-06-inversion-orientation-diagram.png){height="420"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/sv-07-inversion-example.png){height="420"}
:::
::::

Both mates on the **same strand** (→→ or ←←) at each breakpoint — here in the *APP* gene

## Hands-on: find the inversion

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/sv-09-hands-on-inversion-exercise.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. [File > Open Session…]{.menu}
   `igvData/svs/svs_session.xml`
2. Right-click reads → **View as pairs**
3. Look for a cluster of discordant, same-strand pairs

::: {.small .muted}
`NA19240` — a heavily studied 1000 Genomes / HapMap sample
:::
:::
::::

## Your turn: inversion or deletion? {.exercise}

::: {.task}
Both deletions and inversions can drop coverage at their breakpoints.

What *extra* evidence in this view says **inversion**?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
The **orientation** colouring. Deletions give normally-oriented pairs that are too far apart (red). Inversions give **same-strand** pairs (teal / dark blue) — a change in orientation, not just distance.
:::

. . .

::: {.small .muted}
SV callers (Delly, Manta, Lumpy) automate exactly this search genome-wide and output a VCF.
:::

# Long-Read Sequencing {.section-slide background-color="#13294b"}

[Episode 09 · optional]{.ep-num}

[How does IGV handle PacBio and Nanopore reads?]{.ep-q}

## Long reads are noisy

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/longread-01-pacbio-illumina-comparison.png)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **10–100 kb** reads (vs. a few hundred bp)
- Higher **per-read** error rate
- Errors average out in the consensus

<br>

PacBio (top) is covered in small indels that Illumina (bottom) doesn't show.
:::
::::

## Filter the noise

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../fig/longread-02-filtered-small-indels.png)

::: {.small .muted}
Hide small indels
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../fig/longread-03-quick-consensus-mode.png)

::: {.small .muted}
Quick consensus mode
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](../fig/longread-04-preferences-alignments-tab.png)

::: {.small .muted}
[View > Preferences > Alignments]{.menu}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
**But:** filtering can hide real rare variants — always check the unfiltered view before making a call.
:::

## Mapping quality & split reads {.pair}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/longread-06-simple-alignment-detail.png){height="330"}

**MAPQ** (0–255): how sure is the aligner? Low single digits = 🚩
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../fig/longread-07-structural-variant-deletion.png){height="330"}

**Split reads**: one long read spans the whole 6 kb deletion
:::
::::

::: {.small .muted}
Nanopore examples © Oxford Nanopore Technologies, from EPI2ME's "A guide to reviewing BAM files"
:::

## Hands-on: stream remote data

[File > Load from URL…]{.menu} — IGV fetches only the region you view (and finds the index)

::: {.url}
https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/giab/ftp/data/AshkenazimTrio/HG002_NA24385_son/Ultralong_OxfordNanopore/combined_2018-05-18/combined_2018-05-18.hg38.sorted.cram
:::

::: {.url}
https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/giab/ftp/data/AshkenazimTrio/HG002_NA24385_son/UCSC_Ultralong_OxfordNanopore_Promethion/HG002_GRCh38_ONT-UL_UCSC_20200508.phased.bam
:::

1. Genome **Human hg38**, load both URLs
2. Go to `chr20:10,804,515-10,811,999`
3. On the `combined_2018-05-18` track: **Link supplementary alignments** and **Color by › Read strand**

## An inversion inside single reads

![](../fig/longread-09-hg002-inversion-hands-on.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

::: {.small style="text-align:center"}
Reads switch from [pink (forward)]{style="color:#d6477f;font-weight:700"} to [purple (reverse)]{style="color:#7b4fb0;font-weight:700"} and back — no read pairs needed
:::

## Your turn: long-read inversion {.exercise}

::: {.task}
1. Estimate the two **breakpoints** from the colour switch.
2. On the `phased.bam` track: **Color by › Tag** `HP` (and **Group by › Tag** `HP`). Is the inversion on **one haplotype or both**?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment}
Breakpoints ≈ `chr20:10,807,800` and `10,808,450`. Inversion reads in only one HP group → **heterozygous**; in both → **homozygous**. Unphased data can't tell you which.
:::

## Haplotype phasing

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../fig/longread-08-haplotype-phasing.png)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Long reads span several variants on the **same molecule** → tools like WhatsHap tag each read with its haplotype (`HP`)

<br>

*FMR1* repeat expansion: one allele has a small insertion, the other a **much larger** one

::: {.small .muted}
Grey = reads that couldn't be assigned

# Wrap Up {.section-slide background-color="#0f8b8d"}

[Episode 10]{.ep-num}

## What we covered {.keypoints}

- Load genomes — hosted, or your own **FASTA** + **BED**
- Navigate: whole genome → chromosome → region → base pair
- Sort, colour & **BLAT** reads to separate real SNPs from artifacts
- Precompute coverage with **igvtools**
- Splice junctions & **Sashimi plots** for alternative splicing
- **VCF** genotypes grouped by population
- Insert size & orientation reveal **structural variants**
- Long reads: filtering, split reads, **haplotype phasing**

## Where next?

:::: {.columns}

**SV callers** — Delly, Manta, Lumpy → VCF you can view in IGV

**igv.js & IGV-Web** — embed or share views, no install

**Batch scripts** — [Tools > Run Batch Script…]{.menu} for snapshots across many loci
:::

**Video tutorials**
